title: Timberwolves at Stolberg
pull: Trained to fight in the dark

facts.text: On 16 and 17 November 1944 the 104th Infantry Division, the Timberwolves, attacked northeast of Stolberg, Germany, as the left wing of VII Corps in the big November offensive that followed Operation Queen.
Its commander, Maj. Gen. Terry Allen, had led the 1st Infantry Division in North Africa and Sicily until he was replaced in August 1943. He took over the 104th on 15 October 1943.
Allen drilled the division in night attacks. Gen. Omar Bradley later wrote that Allen brought "the only division I know of that was prepared for night combat."
The division had its first combat with the First Canadian Army in Belgium and Holland in October 1944, then took over old 1st Division positions around Stolberg.

Its main objective was the Donnerberg, Hill 287, a height beside Stolberg that had already beaten off earlier American attacks. Mines, barbed wire and three giant pillboxes guarded it, and German artillery watched from the top.

On 16 November the division's artillery fired only 271 rounds. For 17 November General Allen set the attack for noon with a detailed artillery plan and fighter bombers, and his guns fired 5,621 rounds.
Even so the 414th Infantry made little headway on 17 November. A battalion of the 415th Infantry held a toehold in Birkengang, an industrial suburb of Stolberg.
The corps commander, Maj. Gen. J. Lawton Collins, had told the division on 16 November "to get moving and get moving fast."

Around noon on 18 November the German defense cracked and two of the big pillboxes surrendered. That night, in the kind of attack Allen had trained for, one company slipped almost 1,000 yards through the dark Eschweiler woods to seize a road junction.
Tanks of the 750th Tank Battalion fought alongside the Timberwolves in the drive to the Roer, and on 22 November the division's infantry were clearing Eschweiler house by house.

photoNote: US Army Signal Corps photo by Carolan, 22 November 1944: men of Company C, 1st Battalion, 104th Infantry Division search houses in a farmyard in Eschweiler after its capture; the Timberwolf patch is visible on the right hand soldier's shoulder. SC 196557, US Army work, public domain (Commons, from the Signal Corps Archive Flickr scan of the NARA print; FlickreviewR confirmed PD Mark). 1920 x 1634 thumbnail; full file 3587 x 3053 on Commons. Taken five days after the card date, a few miles northeast of Stolberg, same offensive; caption must give 22 November. No NARA 111-SC photo of Terry Allen or of the 104th dated 16 to 17 November was found (NARA search returned nothing usable; the only Allen portrait on Commons is 196 px). Frame on the soldiers in the middle; the number '196557 SA' is bottom left.
photoCredit: Soldiers of the 104th Infantry Division search houses in Eschweiler, Germany, 22 November 1944. US Army Signal Corps SC 196557, public domain.

declassified.fact: The Germans fought back with ammunition they were hoarding for something bigger. On 17 November their LXXXI Corps fired 13,200 artillery rounds, an abnormally high figure, thanks partly to a one time issue from the Fuhrer Reserve, ammunition stockpiled for the coming Ardennes offensive. From the next day they were held to 8,000 rounds.
